9
A parachutist falls vertically from rest at time t = 0 from a hot-air balloon. She falls for some
distance before opening her parachute.
Which graph best shows the variation with time t of the speed v of the parachutist?
A
B

hints: Notice the wording falls vertically from rest at $t=0$, so the $v$ against $t$ curve must start at the origin $(0,0)$.
Recall that gradient of a $v$-$t$ graph is acceleration, and air resistance grows with speed so resultant downward force and acceleration shrink toward first terminal velocity.
Think what opening the parachute does to drag area: drag jumps up, speed must drop steeply and then level off at a second much lower terminal velocity before landing.
walkthrough: Start from the given initial condition: from rest means $v=0$ at $t=0$, so the graph must begin at the origin. This rules out graphs starting at high $v$.
During free fall, weight acts down and drag acts up with drag increasing as $v$ increases. Resultant force $F = mg - D$ decreases, so acceleration $a = F/m$ decreases.

On a $v$-$t$ graph $a$ is the gradient, so $v$ rises steeply at first then with ever-decreasing gradient until $D = mg$ and $a = 0$. That is a curve flattening to a horizontal first terminal velocity.
When the parachute opens, effective area jumps so $D$ becomes much larger than $mg$. The parachutist decelerates strongly, so $v$ drops with a steep negative gradient.
As $v$ falls, $D$ falls until a new balance $D = mg$ at a much lower speed, so the curve flattens again to a low horizontal line until landing. This is option A.

A.explanation: Starts at $v=0$ at $t=0$, rises with decreasing gradient to a first terminal velocity, then falls rapidly when the parachute opens to a lower constant terminal velocity.

B.explanation: Shows an initial straight line of constant gradient, which would mean constant acceleration and ignores increasing air resistance as speed builds up.

C.explanation: Starts at a large non-zero $v$ at $t=0$ and ends at $v=0$ in the air, which contradicts falling from rest and landing with non-zero speed.

D.explanation: Starts at maximum $v$ at $t=0$ and decreases, which contradicts starting from rest with $v=0$.
